records.name: House of Liechtenstein (Princes of Liechtenstein)
records.scaleNote: The family wholly owns LGT, which reported CHF 386.1bn of client assets under management at end-2025, and the Bloomberg Billionaires Index put Hans-Adam II at about US$9.2bn in September 2023.
records.lifespan: 1608 princely rank; 1719 principality; bank from c. 1930; present
records.origins: An Austrian noble family that rose in Habsburg service; Karl I was raised to prince in 1608. In 1699 and 1712 it bought the lordships of Schellenberg and Vaduz, which became the Principality of Liechtenstein in 1719. For three centuries most of its wealth lay in vast estates in Moravia, Bohemia, Silesia and Lower Austria.
records.role_summary: Karl I, as Habsburg governor of Bohemia after the Battle of the White Mountain (1620), oversaw the confiscation of rebel Protestant estates and acquired large ones himself at low cost, plus the Silesian duchy of Jägerndorf (1622). Those estates, worked under serf labour until 1848, were the core of the fortune until Czechoslovakia confiscated them in 1945. The family then rebuilt its wealth around a small Vaduz bank it had bought around 1930, which Hans-Adam II turned into LGT, now one of Europe's largest family-owned private banks.

roleDetail.d: Karl I of Liechtenstein, a convert to Catholicism and an adviser to the Habsburgs, was made a prince in 1608.

As governor and viceroy of Bohemia after the White Mountain, Karl I personally carried out many confiscations, letting the family acquire large Bohemian and Moravian estates cheaply; in 1622 he received Jägerndorf and confiscated 'rebel property'. Historians debate how far he acted on Ferdinand II's orders or on his own initiative.

roleDetail.t: A tiny sovereign state bought with land money (1699–1719).
roleDetail.d: The purchase of Schellenberg and Vaduz gave the family a seat in the Imperial Diet; Emperor Charles VI united them as the Principality of Liechtenstein in 1719.

Under the Beneš decrees Czechoslovakia confiscated the family's property, on the ground that Franz Joseph II had declared German nationality; restitution claims in Czech courts and at the ICJ and ECHR have failed or remain unresolved.

The family bought the Bank in Liechtenstein, founded 1921, around 1930. Hans-Adam II, prince since 1989, built it into LGT; the 1970 Prince of Liechtenstein Foundation holds LGT and an agriculture, forestry and real-estate group.

records.legacy: The money now sits in two arms held through the Prince of Liechtenstein Foundation (Vaduz, 1970): LGT Group, the private bank, and the Liechtenstein Group, which runs forestry in Styria (Forst Kalwang), Austria's largest owner-operated arable farm (Wilfersdorf), the princely wineries, Vienna real estate, RiceTec (US hybrid rice seed), avocado and Uruguayan farming operations. The princely art collections are shown at the two Liechtenstein palaces in Vienna.

legacyDetail.d: LGT reported group profit of CHF 445.6m and client assets of CHF 386.1bn for 2025; the family has controlled it for more than 90 years.
The Liechtenstein Group lists nine portfolio companies across forestry, agriculture, wine, real estate and agri-technology in Austria, Liechtenstein, the US, Spain or Portugal (avocados) and Uruguay.

norman.text: No Norman or 1066 connection. The family is first documented in Lower Austria in the 12th century.

records.name: Thurn und Taxis family (Princes of Thurn and Taxis)
moneySources: Sale of postal rights to Prussia (1867)
records.scaleNote: The family remains Germany's largest private forest owner with nearly 20,000 ha (Euronews, 2026); Forbes valued Albert at about US$1.6bn in 2014.
records.origins: A courier family from Cornello near Bergamo. Franz von Taxis ran the Habsburg courier service between Innsbruck and Brussels from the 1490s, and the family opened the post to paying public customers in the early 1500s. In 1615 Emperor Matthias made the office of Imperial Postmaster General a hereditary fief.
records.role_summary: The fortune was a licence: an imperial monopoly on letter and parcel post across the Holy Roman Empire, run as a family business from c. 1600 to 1806 and, as the Thurn-und-Taxis Post, until 1867. When Napoleon and the 1803 secularisations stripped the family of postal territories, it was compensated with former church lands, including the abbey of St Emmeram in Regensburg and the new Principality of Buchau. In 1867 it sold its postal rights and property to Prussia for three million thaler and recycled the money and rents into estates in Bavaria, Württemberg, Bohemia and Prussian Poland.

roleDetail.d: Franz von Taxis organised the courier link from Innsbruck to the Burgundian Netherlands, and Charles V named Johann Baptista von Taxis Postmaster General in 1517.

The office of Imperial Postmaster General became a hereditary fief; the family became imperial princes in 1695 and moved to Regensburg in 1748 as the Emperor's principal commissioner at the Imperial Diet.

In the secularisations of 1803 the family received the abbey of St Emmeram (which became its residence) and lands forming the Principality of Buchau. It was mediatised in 1806 but kept its private estates.

A treaty of 28 January 1867 transferred the postal rights and property to Prussia for three million thaler, effective 1 July 1867; the family's estates in Bavaria, Württemberg, Prussia and Austria were by area larger than several small German states.

Prince Johannes died in 1990 leaving debts and inheritance tax; TIME (1993) reported a US$40m tax bill. The family sold its bank (1992), held Sotheby's sales at Regensburg (1993), sold the brewery to Paulaner (1996) and sold forest.

records.legacy: The fortune is now land and buildings: nearly 20,000 ha of forest, St Emmeram Palace and its collections, and real estate, run as the Fürst Thurn und Taxis group. The postal business, bank and brewery have all been sold; the brewery brand is licensed to Paulaner.

records.name: House of Wittelsbach (Dukes, Electors and Kings of Bavaria)
moneySources: Royal Civil List and crown estates
records.scaleNote: The Wittelsbacher Ausgleichsfonds was valued at €444m in 2018 by the Bavarian Finance Ministry, excluding art, and pays family line heads about €14m a year.
records.origins: Counts of Scheyern-Wittelsbach who were granted the duchy of Bavaria by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa in 1180 after Henry the Lion was deposed. They ruled Bavaria, and for long periods the Palatinate, until 1918, becoming Electors (1623) and Kings of Bavaria (1806).
records.role_summary: The fortune was the property of a ruling dynasty: crown lands, palaces, forests and collections accumulated over seven centuries, enlarged when Bavaria absorbed secularised church lands and imperial cities in 1803 and became a kingdom under Napoleon in 1806. After the 1918 revolution the Free State and the family negotiated a settlement: in 1923 a public-law foundation, the Wittelsbacher Ausgleichsfonds (WAF), received forests, castles and Munich property, whose income goes to the family, while the state kept most palaces and the art.

roleDetail.d: Otto of Wittelsbach received the duchy from Frederick Barbarossa; the dynasty ruled it for 738 years.
Bavaria absorbed bishoprics, abbeys and free cities, including Regensburg in 1810, and became a kingdom in 1806.
After failed negotiations, the 1923 law created the WAF as an independent public-law foundation; if the entitled family lines die out its assets fall to the Bavarian state.
About 43,000 cultural objects owned by the WAF are on loan to Bavarian state museums.

records.legacy: The family's main wealth vehicle is the WAF: about 12,000 ha of forest, Berg and Grünau castles, central Munich real estate and the Hirschgarten beer garden, plus art lent to state museums. Distributions of about €14m a year go to the heads of the family lines, and the family also holds private assets.

legacyDetail.t: A public-law fund for one family.
legacyDetail.d: The Bavarian Finance Ministry valued the WAF at €348m (2016) and €444m (2018), excluding art.
Press reports note the fund is exempt from audit by the Bavarian Supreme Court of Audit; the state says distributions are not state payments.

records.name: House of Grimaldi (Princes of Monaco)
moneySources: French indemnity for Menton and Roquebrune (1861)
records.scaleNote: Forbes put Albert II at about US$1bn in 2011; no authoritative later estimate was found.
records.origins: A Genoese patrician family; François Grimaldi seized the Rock of Monaco in 1297. The line continued through the female line in 1731 when Jacques Goyon de Matignon took the name and arms.
records.role_summary: Monaco's rulers lived on the rents of a tiny state until 1861, when France paid four million francs for Menton and Roquebrune, about four-fifths of the territory. Charles III then licensed the gaming concession to François Blanc's Société des Bains de Mer (1863), whose casino revenues paid for the principality and let it abolish direct taxes. The prince's own fortune grew alongside a state funded by gaming, banking and property.

roleDetail.d: François Grimaldi took the fortress in 1297; Honoré II was the first to use the title Prince (1612).
By the Franco-Monegasque treaty of 2 February 1861 the prince gave up claims to Menton and Roquebrune for an indemnity of four million francs.
Charles III approved François Blanc's Société des Bains de Mer et du Cercle des Étrangers in 1863; the concession made the casino the principality's main revenue source.

Albert II's lawyer told AFP in 2024 that 'offshore companies were indeed created in Panama in 1984 in the time of Rainier III' and in the British Virgin Islands in 2002, and that 'all this is being liquidated'.

records.legacy: The SBM, which runs the casinos and grand hotels, is majority-owned by the State of Monaco, not by the prince personally, with LVMH and Galaxy Entertainment each having taken 5% in 2015. The prince's private wealth sits in property in Monaco and France, art and investments managed by the Administrator of the Prince's Assets.

legacyDetail.t: State, not family, owns the casino.
legacyDetail.d: The Monegasque state held about 59.7% of SBM after the 2015 LVMH and Galaxy deals; SBM reported revenue of €768m for 2024/25.

records.name: House of Orange-Nassau (Dutch royal family)
records.scaleNote: Quote magazine estimated the family's fortune at about €950m in 2017; Forbes cut its estimate from US$2.5bn (2002) to US$250m (2003) after Prince Bernhard sent details of holdings.
records.origins: German counts of Nassau who inherited the Principality of Orange and large Netherlandish estates in 1544 (William the Silent). They led the Dutch Revolt and held the stadtholderate; William I became king in 1815.
records.role_summary: After 1815 King William I was one of Europe's richest monarchs and steered colonial trade: he founded the Nederlandsche Handel-Maatschappij (1824) to run trade with the East Indies, the era of spice, coffee and tea trading that Newsweek identifies as the root of the modern fortune. In the 20th century the family's investments were long reported to include a large holding in Royal Dutch Shell; TIME wrote it was once thought to own as much as a quarter. Since 1972 the king, his predecessor and heir have been exempt from inheritance and gift tax.

roleDetail.d: William of Nassau inherited Orange and the Breda and other estates; the family's power rested on these lands and the stadtholderate.
William I created the NHM by royal decree to revive East Indies trade; its successors merged into ABN (1964) and later ABN AMRO.

TIME (2002) said the family was 'once thought' to own up to a quarter of Royal Dutch/Shell; Newsweek reported Bernhard's 2003 letter to Forbes detailed holdings in Shell and ABN AMRO. The family never published the stake.
The king, his predecessor and his heir are exempt from gift and inheritance tax, so assets such as the De Horsten estate passed tax-free from Beatrix to Willem-Alexander.

records.legacy: The private fortune is invested in an undisclosed portfolio, the De Horsten estate and other property, and family members' business interests. Functional royal assets (art, jewels, the Golden Coach) sit in seven foundations, mostly chaired by the king, and pass to the successor tax-free; the palaces are state property.

legacyDetail.d: NOS reports the king's 'functional' assets are held in seven stichtingen, in most cases directed by the king.
Juliana's four children and their descendants share the private capital, which NOS says is increasingly fragmented.

records.name: Leopold II, King of the Belgians
records.scaleNote: Leopold's personal profit from Congo rubber in 1896–1905 has been estimated at about 70 million Belgian francs (Wikipedia, citing historians), and the Royal Trust he endowed holds about 7,500 ha valued at at least €231.4m (2022 balance sheet).
aliases: Sovereign of the Congo Free State
records.origins: Second king of the Belgians (r. 1865–1909) of the house of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. Convinced that Belgium needed a colony, he set up the International African Association (1876) and hired Henry Morton Stanley, presenting the venture as humanitarian and anti-slavery.
records.role_summary: At the Berlin Conference era (1884–85) Leopold obtained recognition of the Congo Free State as his personal possession, not Belgium's. From the 1890s he reserved vast areas as state and crown domain (the Domaine de la Couronne, c. 250,000 km²) and extracted rubber and ivory through forced labour enforced by the Force Publique, with killings, hostage-taking and mutilation; domain revenue rose from about 150,000 francs in 1890 to over 18 million by 1901. He spent the profits on buildings and parks in Belgium and gave many of them to the nation in 1900 as the Royal Trust, before ceding the Congo to Belgium in 1908 under international pressure.

roleDetail.t: A colony owned by one man (1885).
roleDetail.d: The Congo Free State was Leopold's personal property from 1885 until Belgium annexed it on 15 November 1908.
Quotas were enforced by the Force Publique; estimates of population decline range from about 1 to 10+ million and are debated, with disease a major cause.

Historians cited in Wikipedia estimate Leopold's personal profit from rubber at about 70 million francs in 1896–1905; Adam Hochschild's estimate is at least c. US$1.1bn in today's money (both approximate).
His 1900 letters gave castles, parks and land to the nation as the Royal Trust, accepted by law in 1903, with more added by a law of 18 October 1908 after the Congo handover.

records.legacy: Leopold's Congo money is still visible in Belgium: the Royal Trust (Donation royale) owns about 7,500 ha, 77 buildings including Laeken park, the Royal Greenhouses and castles used by the royal family, valued at at least €231.4m in its first balance sheet (2022). Much of the rest went into Brussels and Ostend monuments and the Tervuren museum.

legacyDetail.t: Royal Trust properties used by the family.
legacyDetail.d: They include the Belvédère (Albert II), Ciergnon and Fenffe castles, Villa Clémentine (Prince Laurent) and Villa Schonenberg (Princess Astrid).
King Philippe expressed his 'deepest regrets' for colonial violence on 30 June 2020.

wealth.publishedNote: No published figure for Leopold's estate at death was found in a reputable source. Historians' profit estimates are given in roleDetail.

records.scaleNote: Austria's 1919 Habsburg Law transferred the court and family-fund assets to the Republic; no reliable published valuation of the family's remaining private wealth exists.
records.lifespan: 1278–1918 rulers of Austria; Holy Roman Emperors 1438–1806 (almost continuously); present
records.base: Vienna (historic); family seats in Austria and Bavaria
records.origins: Counts from the Aargau (Habsburg castle, Switzerland). Rudolf I was elected King of the Romans in 1273 and won Austria and Styria from Ottokar II of Bohemia in 1278. Through marriages the dynasty gathered Burgundy and the Netherlands, Spain and its Indies, and Bohemia and Hungary.
records.role_summary: Habsburg wealth was the wealth of states: crown domains, mines (Tyrolean silver, Bohemian and Hungarian ores), tolls, and the revenues of an empire built by marriage more than war. The dynasty was also the great distributor of land: after 1620 it confiscated Protestant Bohemian estates and granted or sold them to loyal nobles such as the Liechtensteins. In 1919 the Austrian Republic took the court property and the entailed Habsburg family fund, leaving only demonstrably private assets.

roleDetail.d: Rudolf I's victory over Ottokar II at the Marchfeld gave the family Austria, its core for 640 years.
Marriages brought Burgundy (1477), Castile and Aragon with the Indies (1496–1516) and Bohemia and Hungary (1526).
After the White Mountain the crown confiscated rebel estates and transferred them to Catholic loyalists, enriching houses such as Liechtenstein.

The Habsburg Law of 3 April 1919 transferred court and family-fund property to the Republic; it remains in constitutional force and is confirmed by the 1955 State Treaty. Repeated restitution claims have failed.

records.legacy: The former imperial palaces, collections and family-fund estates belong to the Republic of Austria (run by bodies such as the Schönbrunn company and the federal forests) and the City of Vienna. The family keeps undisclosed private assets; branches hold estates in Austria, Bavaria, Spain and elsewhere.

records.lifespan: 1415 Electors of Brandenburg; 1701–1918 Kings of Prussia; 1871–1918 German Emperors; present
records.origins: Swabian counts who became burgraves of Nuremberg and, in 1415, Electors of Brandenburg. The Franconian-Brandenburg line became Kings in Prussia (1701) and German Emperors (1871–1918); the Catholic Swabian line kept Sigmaringen and Hechingen.
records.role_summary: The Prussian line's wealth was the crown domain of a growing state, plus the Great Elector's 1682 Brandenburg African Company, which historians estimate shipped up to c. 20,000 Africans. After 1918 Prussia and the dynasty settled in 1926, leaving ownership of many objects open; the Soviet zone's 1945 land reform took most remaining eastern property. The Sigmaringen line, never a sovereign of Prussia, kept its Swabian forests and built an industrial group around the Zollern foundry (founded 1708).

roleDetail.d: Burgrave Frederick VI of Nuremberg was enfeoffed with Brandenburg by Emperor Sigismund.
The Great Elector chartered the Brandenburg African Company; Frederick William I sold Groß Friedrichsburg to the Dutch WIC in 1717 for c. 7,000 ducats and 12 enslaved Africans.
After the national referendum on expropriating the princes failed on turnout in June 1926, Prussia concluded a treaty with the house that left ownership of many art objects open.
The Sigmaringen head holds 50% of the engineering group founded in 1708, alongside forests, DIY stores, real estate and a ski area (Schwäbische Zeitung).

records.legacy: Prussian line: Burg Hohenzollern (shared), residual art and a seat on the 2025 public Hohenzollern Art Collection Foundation (6:3 public-to-family board). Sigmaringen line: c. 15,000 ha of forest, Sigmaringen Castle, real estate, and a 50% stake in the Zollern engineering group.

trails.title: From the imperial post to Germany's largest private forest
trails.summary: A Lombard courier family turned a Habsburg contract into a hereditary monopoly, was compensated with church lands when the Empire collapsed, cashed out to Prussia in 1867 and put the money into land. After the 1990 death duties the family sold its bank, brewery and art, and is left mainly with forest and the Regensburg palace.

steps.title: Courier contract
steps.text: Franz von Taxis organised the Habsburg courier line between Innsbruck and the Netherlands.

source.label: Thurn und Taxis — History of the family

steps.title: Hereditary monopoly
steps.text: The Imperial Postmaster Generalship became a hereditary fief of the family.

steps.title: Move to Regensburg
steps.text: Alexander Ferdinand became the Emperor's principal commissioner at the Imperial Diet in Regensburg.

source.label: Wikipedia — House of Thurn und Taxis

steps.title: Compensated with church land
steps.text: The secularisations gave the family St Emmeram Abbey in Regensburg and the Principality of Buchau.

source.label: Wikipedia — House of Thurn und Taxis

steps.title: Sale to Prussia
steps.text: The postal rights and property were sold to Prussia for three million thaler; the family had already bought estates in Bavaria, Tyrol and Bohemia.

steps.title: Death duties
steps.text: Prince Johannes died; TIME reported a US$40m tax bill. The bank was sold in 1992, c. 4,000 lots auctioned in 1993 and the brewery sold to Paulaner in 1996.

steps.title: Today: forest and a palace
steps.text: The family holds nearly 20,000 ha of forest, Germany's largest private forest holding, plus St Emmeram and real estate.

trails.title: From Congo rubber to the Belgian Royal Trust
trails.summary: Leopold II ran the Congo as his personal property, extracted rubber through forced labour, spent the profits on Belgian buildings and land, and locked them into a Royal Trust whose properties the royal family still uses.

steps.title: A colony owned by one man
steps.text: The Congo Free State was recognised as Leopold II's personal possession.

source.label: Wikipedia — Atrocities in the Congo Free State

steps.title: Crown domain and forced rubber
steps.text: Leopold reserved the c. 250,000 km² Domaine de la Couronne; forced rubber collection enforced by the Force Publique raised domain revenue to over 18 million francs by 1901.

source.label: Wikipedia — Atrocities in the Congo Free State

steps.title: Gift to the nation
steps.text: Leopold's 1900 letters gave castles, parks and land to Belgium on condition they never be sold and stay available to his successors; accepted by law in 1903.

steps.title: Personal profits
steps.text: Historians estimate Leopold's personal rubber profit in 1896–1905 at about 70 million francs.

source.label: Wikipedia — Atrocities in the Congo Free State

steps.title: Handover and more property
steps.text: Belgium annexed the Congo; a law of 18 October 1908 added further properties to the Trust.

steps.title: Autonomous public institution
steps.text: A royal decree made the Royal Trust an autonomous public body.

steps.title: Today: first valuation
steps.text: The Trust's first balance sheet valued its c. 7,500 ha and 77 buildings at about €231m; castles and villas are used by members of the royal family.

source.label: BRF — Erste Schätzung von Wert der königlichen Schenkung von Leopold II. (7 Jan 2024, citing La Libre Belgique)
